extracted.intended_audience: journal referees and authors in computer science / mathematics (graduate students, faculty, and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for referees and authors on reviewing, preparing, and presenting mathematical/computer-science papers: how to decide accept/reject, what items to check (correctness, contribution, bibliography, English), how to handle illustrations, and how to write/organize proofs and notation for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee decision categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers generally will fall into the following categories: (1) Publish essentially as is; (2) Publish after author's minor revision; (3) Publish only if the author makes major revision; (4) Reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals use checkbox ratings: e.g. 'accept', 'accept with major modifications', 'accept with minor changes', 'Reject: submit to ______'. When rejecting, referees may be asked to suggest a less prestigious journal that might publish the work. The system of downward filtering means even weak papers may find a venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: The goals of a referee are to keep the quality of publication as high as possible and also to help the author to produce a better paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reports designed to give the author maximum benefit while not compromising on quality. Treat refereeing as an important professional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to the state of the art (or clearly labelled expository)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should contribute to the state of the art; if it is purely expository it should be clearly designated as expository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the manuscript makes a genuine technical or conceptual contribution; if it is expository, it must be honest about that role rather than masquerading as original research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: All technical material must be correct (i.e. no incorrect equations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check details carefully; point out subtle technical errors. In some cases the author may need to run computations or write programs to confirm or refute alleged mistakes. If errors are found, explain them and whether they are fatal or fixable.

rubrics_metrics.name: English style and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: The article must be readable and well written; English style matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out misleading or overly subtle presentation, typographic errors, and notation choices that impede understanding. Referees often recommend notation changes and stylistic improvements to aid clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The bibliography should be adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that prior relevant work is cited; supply missing references when possible. Lack of appropriate references is a common failing, especially when an author ventures outside their usual field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and report submission protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should return reports promptly and follow submission protocol: return the manuscript to the editor (do not mark it up) and submit the report in duplicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid postponing the review; typical expectations (here) mention about four weeks. Remember the publication cycle: delays can block progress. Submit duplicate copies so one can be routed to the author; do not scribble corrections on the manuscript itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential correspondence and separate editor letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee identities are usually hidden from authors; if desired, write an accompanying confidential letter to the editor but do not include it as the referee's report to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the referee's report separate from any confidential comments to the editor. If you want the editor to know your identity or private assessment, communicate that as a separate letter rather than in the report that will be sent to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive, specific feedback (references, notation, enjoyable/weak sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should give constructive specific comments: point out enjoyed sections, suggest notation changes, list references, highlight misleading exposition, and identify substantive improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concrete: provide references the author missed, cite specific paragraphs or equations that need change, and indicate which parts are particularly good. Helpful comments may lead to new ideas for the author; aim to improve the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid facile generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not propose 'facile generalizations' — generalizations that are merely mechanical manipulations of a given argument without creating new insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When suggesting extensions, ensure they add conceptual value rather than being trivial formal variants of existing results. Calling out trivial suggestions helps keep feedback substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing as cooperative professional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing is a cooperative effort — a correspondence between many world authorities; referees may improve others' papers as they help with theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to invest effort to improve papers. Be mindful that substantive anonymous contributions may be significant; in rare cases, a referee might choose to publish a competing paper rather than merely be acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title clarity / avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose unambiguous titles; reviewers should point out titles that admit multiple readings (examples: 'Optimal Font Caching' could mean caching of optimal fonts or the optimal method for font caching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a title can be parsed multiple ways, suggest an explicit clearer title. Small changes in wording can eliminate confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: keep them small and appropriately detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small; detailed figures can serve those who want detail while remaining ignorable by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer compact, focused diagrams. If detailed figures are necessary, organize them so casual readers can ignore the minutiae while experts can inspect details. Note: preparing illustrations can be expensive in effort (humorously noted as proportional to the cube of the number of illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data rather than cooked 'sample' data
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to use 'real' data than 'sample data' that have been cooked up solely to use as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real examples give more convincing evidence of algorithm behavior and exposition; avoid contrived examples that merely showcase a point in an artificial way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color and illustrations by medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can be used effectively in talks, but usually not in papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the intended medium: color slides for talks may aid comprehension, but printed papers often do not support color affordably; plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and alignment of text and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange final text opposite the diagrams to which it refers; tables and diagrams should be placed so the reader can easily correlate them with explanatory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clarity, ensure figures and the corresponding descriptive text appear near each other (opposite pages in books, inline in articles). Use tables when numerical data present ideas that are not easily shown graphically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical comparisons and statistical displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Use histograms or other statistical displays to illustrate algorithm performance, but beware of biases (e.g., author's tendency to rewrite ugly examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting empirical evidence, disclose potential biases in data selection and be transparent about experimental setup and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation simplicity: minimize subscripts/superscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for notation that needs no double subscripts or subscripted superscripts; simplify notation so there are no subscripted subscripts or subscripted superscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast proofs and definitions to reduce nested notation. Hold back unnecessary notation until needed; use words when they are clearer than heavy symbolic notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-exposition techniques (factor, orient, 'hold back')
rubrics_metrics.description: Good proof exposition techniques include 'holding back' before enumerating elements, factoring the proof into subgoals, telling the reader the overall method (e.g. 'this is essentially a diagonalization technique'), and simplifying by using words rather than heavy notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor proofs so each piece has a simple interface, reducing reader memory load. Give orientation statements to help readers grasp the strategy before the details. Address edge cases/initialization explicitly for readers unaccustomed to empty constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and acknowledgements ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly acknowledge contributors and list coauthors; young authors frequently overlook proper acknowledgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure credit is given where due (coauthors, student contributions, technical help). Omitting acknowledgements is a common mistake; conversely, appropriate attribution is professionally important.
